chunks: He was asked about a Muslim man who dies while traveling, and there is no Muslim man with him, but there are Christian men with him, and his paternal aunt and maternal aunt are two Muslim women. How should his ghusl be carried out? He said: “His paternal aunt and maternal aunt should wash him while he is in his shirt, and the Christians should not approach him.”

And about a woman who dies while traveling, and there is no Muslim woman with her, but there are Christian women with her, and her paternal uncle and maternal uncle are two Muslim men, he said: “They should wash her, and the Christian woman should not approach her, except that there should be a garment upon her, then water should be poured from above the garment.”

key_terms.السَّفَرِ: travel, the circumstance in which this exceptional ruling applies
key_terms.النَّصَارَى: the Christians, who are not to approach the deceased in this case
key_terms.خَالَتُهُ: his maternal aunt, a close female relative permitted here to wash him
key_terms.دِرْعٌ: a garment covering the woman's body during washing
key_terms.عَمَّتُهُ: his paternal aunt, a close female relative permitted here to wash him
key_terms.غُسْلِهِ: the ritual washing of the deceased man's body
key_terms.فَيُصَبُّ الْمَاءُ: water is poured over the garment rather than direct bodily contact
key_terms.يُغَسِّلَانِهَا: the two men wash her, referring to her paternal and maternal uncles

ai.seo_question: How should the deceased Muslim be washed during travel if no same-sex Muslim is present?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a fiqh ruling for washing a deceased Muslim during travel when a same-sex Muslim washer is unavailable. It permits certain close mahram relatives to perform the ghusl with a barrier of clothing, while excluding non-Muslims from handling the body.
